lessons.title: Identifying Common Tomato Pests
lessons.body: To manage pests, you must first know your enemy. In Africa, the most destructive tomato pests are: African bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera), whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci), aphids, spider mites, thrips, and leafminers. African bollworm larvae are green or brown, up to 4 cm long, with light stripes. They bore holes into fruits and feed on leaves. Check for dark frass (droppings) near holes. Whiteflies are tiny (1-2 mm), white, and cluster under leaves. When you shake a plant, they fly up in a cloud. They transmit tomato yellow leaf curl virus. Aphids are small (2-3 mm), green, black, or red, and cluster on new shoots. They secrete honeydew, which attracts ants and sooty mold. Spider mites are red or brown, barely visible, and spin fine webs on the undersides of leaves. Thrips are slender, 1-2 mm, and cause silvery streaks on leaves and fruits. Leafminers are small flies whose larvae tunnel inside leaves, leaving winding white trails. Scout your field twice a week, early morning or late afternoon. Walk in a zigzag pattern, inspect 10 plants per row, and look at the top and bottom of leaves, stems, and fruits. Carry a hand lens (10x) and a notebook. Record which pests you see and their numbers. For example, if you find 5 or more whiteflies per leaf, you need to act. Early detection saves your crop.

lessons.title: Integrated Pest Management (IPM) Strategies
lessons.body: IPM is a smart, cost-effective way to control pests by combining methods: cultural, physical, biological, and chemical (as a last resort). Start with cultural controls. Rotate crops: do not plant tomatoes where you grew tomatoes, peppers, or potatoes in the last 2-3 years. This breaks pest life cycles. Plant resistant varieties like 'Tanya' or 'Moneymaker' if available. Sanitation: remove and burn crop debris after harvest. Weeds like black nightshade host aphids and whitefliesâkeep fields clean. Spacing: plant tomatoes 60 cm apart within rows and 1 m between rows to improve airflow and reduce humidity, which discourages fungal diseases and some pests. Stake or trellis plants to keep fruits off the ground, away from soil pests. Physical controls: handpick bollworm and aphids; use a strong jet of water to knock off whiteflies and mites. Mulch with straw or plastic to reduce soil-borne pests. Biological controls: conserve natural enemies like ladybirds, lacewings, and parasitic wasps by avoiding broad-spectrum pesticides. Chemical control: only when pest numbers exceed thresholds. For example, treat African bollworm when you find 1-2 larvae per plant. Use selective pesticides like Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) or neem oil. Rotate chemicals to prevent resistance. Always follow label instructions and wear protective gear. IPM saves money, protects your health, and keeps pests from ruining your harvest.

lessons.title: Biological Controls: Beneficial Insects and Predators
lessons.body: Nature provides free pest control if you encourage it. Beneficial insects eat or parasitize tomato pests. Ladybirds (ladybugs) are your friends. Both adults and larvae eat aphids, whiteflies, and spider mites. One ladybird can eat 50 aphids a day. Lacewing larvae, called 'aphid lions,' are voracious predators of aphids, thrips, and mites. You can buy them from suppliers, but it's cheaper to attract them. Plant flowers like marigolds, sunflowers, and coriander around your tomato field. These provide nectar and pollen for adult beneficials. Parasitic wasps (e.g., Encarsia formosa) lay eggs inside whitefly nymphs, killing them. You can buy cards with parasitized pupae and hang them in the field. Predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis) control spider mites. To keep these helpers, avoid broad-spectrum insecticides like cypermethrin, which kill both pests and beneficials. Use selective products like neem oil or soap sprays, which have less impact. Also, provide shelter: hedgerows and intercropping with maize or beans create habitat. If you must spray, do it in the evening when beneficials are less active. Monitor your field: if you see many ladybirds and few pests, you may not need to spray at all. Biological control is cheap, safe, and sustainable. It takes patience, but it works.

lessons.title: Organic Pesticides and Their Safe Use
lessons.body: Organic pesticides are derived from natural sources and break down quickly, but they are still poisonsâhandle with care. Common ones for tomato pests: Neem oil (from neem tree seeds) controls aphids, whiteflies, thrips, and mites. Mix 5 ml neem oil with 1 L water and a few drops of liquid soap. Spray early morning or evening, covering both sides of leaves. Reapply every 7-10 days. Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is a bacterium that kills bollworm and other caterpillars. Mix according to label (usually 2 g per L water). Spray when larvae are small. It is safe for beneficials. Insecticidal soap (potassium salts of fatty acids) kills soft-bodied pests like aphids and whiteflies by drying them out. Mix 15 ml soap per 1 L water. Spray directly on pests. Pyrethrum (from chrysanthemum flowers) is a broad-spectrum insecticide. Use sparingly as it also kills beneficials. Always wear protective clothing: gloves, mask, long sleeves, and goggles. Never spray in windy conditions. Keep children and animals away. Store pesticides in original labeled containers, locked away from food. Wash hands and clothes after use. Do not spray within 3 days of harvest. Remember, organic does not mean harmless. Follow all safety rules.

lessons.title: Preventing Pest Infestations with Row Covers
lessons.body: Row covers are physical barriers that keep pests off your tomatoes. They are made of lightweight, spun-bonded fabric (e.g., Agribon or Reemay) that allows light, air, and water through but blocks insects. Use them immediately after transplanting or sowing. For tomatoes, you need a cover that is at least 2 m wide and long enough to cover your rows. Drape it over hoops made of wire or PVC to create a tunnel, or lay it directly on the plants and secure the edges with soil, rocks, or sandbags. Ensure there are no gapsâwhiteflies and aphids can crawl through tiny openings. Row covers are most effective against whiteflies, aphids, leafminers, and thrips. They also protect against strong sun, heavy rain, and wind. However, they can increase humidity, which may promote fungal diseases. Monitor and vent on hot days. Remove covers when plants start to flower because bees and other pollinators need access for fruit set. For tomatoes, you can also use covers only during the first 4-6 weeks after transplanting, when plants are most vulnerable. After that, natural enemies can help. Row covers are reusable; clean and store them dry. They cost about $20-$30 for a 10 m roll, but they save on pesticide costs and crop losses. In Africa, they are especially useful during whitefly outbreaks.

lessons.title: Monitoring and Scouting Techniques
lessons.body: Monitoring means regularly checking your crop to detect pests early. Scout your tomato field at least twice a week, starting from transplanting. Walk in a zigzag or 'W' pattern across the field. Stop at 10 random points per hectare. At each point, inspect 5 plants. Look at the upper and lower leaf surfaces, stems, flowers, and fruits. Use a hand lens (10x) to see small pests like mites and thrips. Count pests and record in a notebook. Also note beneficial insects. For whiteflies, gently shake a plant and count how many fly up. For aphids, count colonies on new growth. For bollworm, look for holes in fruits and frass. For spider mites, tap a leaf over a white paperâmites will appear as tiny moving specks. Set action thresholds: e.g., spray only if you find 5 whiteflies per leaf, 10 aphids per leaf, or 2 bollworm larvae per plant. Use yellow sticky traps to monitor whiteflies and aphids. Hang 10 traps per hectare, 30 cm above the canopy. Check traps weekly and replace when full. Pheromone traps for bollworm can help detect moth activity. Record all data in a field diary. This helps you see patterns and decide when to act. Early detection prevents small problems from becoming infestations. Share your findings with other farmers to learn together.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Pest Management for Tomato Farming in Africa

Pest management is not simply about killing insects. For the African tomato farmer, it is a business discipline: every pest outbreak translates directly into lost yield, lower market grade, reduced income, and wasted input costs. This practical reference consolidates the key knowledge from the six lessons in this module into a single, field-ready document. Keep it with your spray records, scout notebook, and input inventory.

Tomatoes (Solanum lycopersicum) are among the most pest-sensitive horticultural crops grown in Africa. A single unprotected season can suffer 40â100% losses from a combination of whiteflies, thrips, fruit borers, and spider mites. The farmer who monitors early, acts on thresholds, and protects natural enemies spends less on chemicals and sells more Grade A fruit.

Key Pest Identification and Damage Reference

The table below summarises the six most economically important tomato pests across sub-Saharan Africa, their damage symptoms, and the monitoring threshold at which intervention becomes profitable. Thresholds are drawn from FAO IPM guidelines and regional research stations.

Table 1: Priority Tomato Pests in Africa â Identification, Damage, and Action Threshold
Pest Key Identification Damage / Business Impact Action Threshold
Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci) 1â2 mm white bodies, cloud of insects when plant disturbed; nymphs on leaf undersides Vectors Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus (TYLCV) â up to 90% yield loss; honeydew causes sooty mould reducing fruit grade 5 adults per leaflet or 2 nymphs per cmÂ²
Thrips (Frankliniella spp.) Slender 1â2 mm insects, yellow-brown to black; jump when disturbed Flower drop, silver scarring on fruit; vectors Tomato Spotted Wilt Virus 10 thrips per flower
Spider Mite (Tetranychus spp.) Microscopic red/brown mites; fine webbing on undersides of leaves Leaf bronzing, defoliation; severe in hot dry season; 30â50% loss 5â10 mites per leaflet or visible webbing
African Bollworm (Helicoverpa armigera) Larvae 30â40 mm, variable colour with dark stripes; bore into fruit Direct fruit destruction; renders fruit unmarketable; secondary rot 1 larva per plant or 2 per 10 plants
Diamondback Moth (Plutella xylostella) Small green larvae 8â12 mm; wiggle when touched; small holes in leaves Defoliation of young plants; stunted growth 5 larvae per plant on seedlings
Leafminer (Liriomyza spp.) Serpentine white tunnels on leaves; small black flies Reduced photosynthesis; significant in greenhouse production 5 active mines per leaf

Source: FAO (2022) Integrated Pest Management for Tomato; CABI (2023) Plantwise Knowledge Bank â Tomato; AVRDC (2019) Tomato Pest Management in the Tropics.

IPM Decision Matrix: Which Tool to Use When

Integrated Pest Management means combining cultural, biological, and chemical tools in a sequence that minimises cost and resistance risk. The matrix below links common field situations to the recommended first-line response, based on the six lessons in this module.

Table 2: IPM Decision Matrix for African Tomato Farms
Field Situation First-Line Action (Low Cost) Second-Line Action Chemical Last Resort
Pre-planting / land prep Solarisation, crop rotation with maize or cereals, remove crop debris Plant resistant or tolerant varieties (e.g., TYLCV-tolerant) Soil drench only if nematode history confirmed
Seedling stage â whitefly present Row covers / insect nets; yellow sticky traps at 20 per acre Release Encarsia formosa parasitic wasps; neem oil spray Imidacloprid only if virus symptoms appear
Flowering â thrips damage Blue sticky traps; avoid excess nitrogen fertiliser Predatory mites (Amblyseius); spinosad (organic-approved) Spinosad or abamectin rotation
Fruiting â bollworm larvae Hand-pick larvae; encourage birds; release Trichogramma wasps Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) spray â safe for beneficials Emamectin benzoate or chlorantraniliprole
Hot dry spell â spider mites Overhead irrigation to raise humidity; remove dusty weeds Predatory mite Phytoseiulus persimilis; insecticidal soap Abamectin â rotate with sulphur
Greenhouse / tunnel production Screening vents; quarantine new seedlings; sanitise tools Banker plants with parasitoids; UV-reflective mulch Targeted spot spray only; never blanket spray

Source: Adapted from FAO (2022) IPM for Tomato; KALRO (2021) Tomato Production Handbook for Kenya; IITA (2020) Integrated Pest Management for Vegetable Crops in West Africa.

â ï¸ SAFETY WARNING â Pesticide Handling

Never spray without Personal Protective Equipment (PPE). At minimum: long-sleeved shirt, long trousers, rubber boots, chemical-resistant gloves, goggles, and a nose/mouth mask. Many African smallholder poisoning cases occur because farmers spray in sandals and shorts.

Pre-harvest interval (PHI) is non-negotiable. If the label says 7 days, do not harvest for 7 days. Selling fruit with pesticide residue destroys buyer trust, can close your market access, and harms consumers. EU and local supermarket buyers routinely test for MRLs (Maximum Residue Limits).

Never mix more than two pesticides. Tank-mixing three or more products increases phytotoxicity risk and is a common cause of crop burn. Always follow label rates â doubling the dose does not double kill; it doubles resistance and cost.

Store pesticides locked away from children, food, and animal feed. Dispose of empty containers by triple-rinsing and puncturing â never reuse for drinking water.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Scout twice weekly. Walk a W-pattern across the field, inspect 10 plants per acre, check leaf undersides and flowers. Record findings in a notebook â this is your early warning system.
  • Know your thresholds. Do not spray on first sight. Use Table 1 above. Spraying below threshold wastes money and kills beneficial insects.
  • Identify before you act. Whitefly, thrips, and mites require different responses. Misdiagnosis is the most expensive mistake in pest management.
  • Protect beneficial insects. Ladybirds, lacewings, and parasitic wasps are free labour. Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides (e.g., lambda-cyhalothrin) unless absolutely necessary.
  • Use row covers on seedlings. Insect netting (0.4â0.8 mm mesh) excludes whitefly and aphids during the first 4â6 weeks â the critical virus infection window.
  • Rotate chemical modes of action. Never spray the same active ingredient twice in a row. Resistance develops fast in whitefly and mites. Keep a spray log with dates and product names.
  • Sanitise between seasons. Remove and burn or compost crop debris. Volunteer tomato plants harbour pests and viruses between crops.
  • Respect PHI and PPE. Your health and your market access depend on it. Keep a record of every spray: date, product, rate, PHI, and safe harvest date.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Integrated Pest Management for Tomato Production (2022) â free PDF, covers thresholds, biological control, and safe pesticide use.
  • CABI Plantwise Knowledge Bank â free pest fact sheets for tomato and other African crops, with photos and management options.
  • IITA â Integrated Pest Management for Vegetable Crops in West Africa (2020) â regional guide with practical field protocols.
  • KALRO â Tomato Production Handbook for Kenya (2021) â includes pest calendars, variety recommendations, and input costs.
  • AVRDC / WorldVeg â Tomato Pest Management in the Tropics (2019) â technical bulletin on resistant varieties and IPM packages.

This practical reference is part of the RISE AFRICA Skills course Tomato Farming â Module: Pest Management. Keep it with your farm records. Review it before every planting season and update your spray log after every application.

quiz.q: What is the scientific name of the African bollworm?
quiz.explanation: Helicoverpa armigera is the African bollworm, a major tomato pest.

quiz.q: Which pest transmits tomato yellow leaf curl virus?
quiz.explanation: Whiteflies (Bemisia tabaci) are vectors of tomato yellow leaf curl virus.

quiz.q: What is a sign of spider mite infestation on tomato leaves?
quiz.explanation: Spider mites spin fine webs on the undersides of leaves.

quiz.q: How often should you scout your tomato field for pests?
quiz.explanation: Scouting twice a week allows early detection and timely action.

quiz.q: Which of these is a cultural control method for tomato pests?
quiz.explanation: Crop rotation breaks pest life cycles and is a cultural control.

quiz.q: What is the recommended spacing for tomato plants to improve airflow?
options: A) 30 cm within rows, 50 cm between rows
B) 60 cm within rows, 1 m between rows
C) 1 m within rows, 1.5 m between rows
D) 20 cm within rows, 40 cm between rows
quiz.explanation: 60 cm within rows and 1 m between rows improves airflow and reduces humidity.

quiz.q: When should you treat African bollworm according to IPM thresholds?
options: A) When you see 1-2 larvae per plant
B) When you see 5 larvae per plant
C) When you see 10 larvae per plant
D) When you see any moth
quiz.explanation: The action threshold for African bollworm is 1-2 larvae per plant.

quiz.q: Which beneficial insect eats aphids, whiteflies, and spider mites?
quiz.explanation: Ladybirds (ladybugs) are generalist predators that eat many soft-bodied pests.

quiz.q: What is the role of flowers like marigolds in biological control?
quiz.explanation: Marigolds provide nectar and pollen for adult beneficial insects.

quiz.q: Which pesticide is a bacterium that kills caterpillars?
quiz.explanation: Bacillus thuringiensis (Bt) is a bacterium toxic to caterpillar larvae.

quiz.q: How should you mix neem oil for spraying?
options: A) 5 ml neem oil + 1 L water + few drops soap
B) 10 ml neem oil + 1 L water
C) 1 ml neem oil + 1 L water
D) 20 ml neem oil + 1 L water
quiz.explanation: The standard neem oil mix is 5 ml per liter of water with a few drops of soap as an emulsifier.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid spraying organic pesticides in the middle of the day?
quiz.explanation: Beneficial insects are most active during the day, so spraying then harms them.

quiz.q: What is a key safety practice when using organic pesticides?
quiz.explanation: Always wear gloves, mask, long sleeves, and goggles when handling pesticides.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of row covers?
quiz.explanation: Row covers are physical barriers that exclude pests like whiteflies and aphids.

quiz.q: When should you remove row covers from tomatoes?
options: B) When plants start to flower
quiz.explanation: Remove covers at flowering to allow pollinators access for fruit set.

quiz.q: What is a disadvantage of using row covers?
quiz.explanation: Row covers can increase humidity, promoting fungal diseases.

quiz.q: How many yellow sticky traps should you hang per hectare?
quiz.explanation: 10 yellow sticky traps per hectare are recommended for monitoring whiteflies and aphids.

quiz.q: What is the action threshold for whiteflies per leaf before spraying?
quiz.explanation: Spray when you find 5 or more whiteflies per leaf.

quiz.q: Which pattern should you use when scouting a tomato field?
quiz.explanation: A zigzag or W pattern ensures you sample different areas of the field.

quiz.q: What tool is useful for seeing small pests like mites and thrips?
quiz.explanation: A 10x hand lens allows you to see tiny pests clearly.

quiz.q: What does frass near a hole in a tomato fruit indicate?
quiz.explanation: Frass (droppings) near holes is a sign of African bollworm feeding.

quiz.q: Which of these is a physical control method?
quiz.explanation: Handpicking is a physical control method.

quiz.q: What is the recommended concentration for insecticidal soap spray?
quiz.explanation: Mix 15 ml of insecticidal soap per 1 L of water.

quiz.q: Which beneficial insect is known as 'aphid lion'?
quiz.explanation: Lacewing larvae are called 'aphid lions' due to their voracious appetite for aphids.

quiz.q: How can you attract beneficial insects to your tomato field?
quiz.explanation: Flowers provide nectar and pollen for adult beneficial insects.

quiz.q: What is the pre-harvest interval for most organic pesticides?
quiz.explanation: Wait at least 3 days after spraying before harvest.

quiz.q: Which pest causes winding white trails on leaves?
quiz.explanation: Leafminer larvae tunnel inside leaves, leaving winding white trails.

quiz.q: What is the first step in IPM?
quiz.explanation: Monitoring and correct identification are the foundation of IPM.

quiz.q: Which of these is a selective pesticide that conserves beneficials?
quiz.explanation: Neem oil is selective and has less impact on beneficial insects.

quiz.q: How many plants should you inspect at each scouting point?
quiz.explanation: Inspect 5 plants per scouting point for a representative sample.
